Cyber in the renewal window

Most small businesses an agency insures have no cyber coverage, and most agents never bring it up. The renewal window is the moment to offer it, but getting a client from "no cyber" to "protected" takes too much manual work, so the moment gets missed.

Prepared for Matt Hightower, David, the executive team and engineeringRandy Hesse

I treated this as a throughput problem disguised as a sales problem. The measure I designed around is agent minutes per bound cyber policy.

Stage 1 · UKON 1Confirm data
Stage 2 · UKON 1Get indications
Stage 3 · UKON 2Client proposal pack
Stage 4 · UKON 3Equip the agent
Stage 5 · UKON 4Questionnaire
Stage 6 · UKON 4Decision, bind, report

I split UKON's Stage 1 in two: confirming the five fields, then the round trip with carriers, with a person's approval in between. Its Stage 4 is split the same way: the questionnaire (often several calls and emails), then the owner's decision, the firm quote, binding and the after-bind plan. The part I prototyped most deeply is UKON's Stage 1 (my Stages 1 and 2), getting a client indication-ready. It's the gate: if an agent has to hand-collect five fields for every renewing client, nothing downstream happens. The prototype then carries one real client, Sloan's Lake Dental in Denver (public data only; agency, calls and carriers simulated), through the later stages to show how that output gets used.

The rule underneath all of it

The database owns the numbers; the wiki owns the evidence. AI reads, extracts, explains and writes prose. It never writes a premium, limit, deductible, or any figure a client sees. People confirm the company match, flagged estimates and call answers, and the client signs the application.
